description: UAE duo, my 4th Space Apps. I build AI tools and data pipelines (Python, React); Yannick leads design, video and storytelling. We’re on Planet X: enter sky coordinates, watch a SPHEREx time-lapse, and spot moving brown dwarfs and asteroids. Our pipeline already pulls live NASA data. We plan before we build and verify every number. Looking for: astronomy knowledge (proper motion, near-IR, variable stars), FITS/Astropy image work, or React/Aladin Lite visualisation.
summary: Waveshift turns NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey into a blink comparator that anyone can use in a browser. Pick a target, or type any coordinates or object name: Waveshift shows the same 2.5-arcminute patch of sky photographed months apart and blinks between the visits, so anything that moved or changed brightness stands out, the technique that found Pluto. Blink tools such as WiseView already do this for WISE; Waveshift brings it to SPHEREx and adds its spectral dimension. Switch between six detector arrays or click any pixel for its spectrum, and see what an object is, not only that it moved. Curated views of Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis load instantly. Any other position is fetched live from NASA’s IRSA archive: a first image appears in under 20 seconds and sharpens as more exposures are stacked. Difference imaging and labelled contamination flags let curious users go deeper, and every number can be checked: Barnard’s Star’s measured shift is 1.68 pixels, against 1.67 predicted from its known motion.
details:
What it does
Waveshift answers one question. What changed in this patch of sky? You can choose one of five curated targets, or enter any RA/Dec or object name. The viewer blinks between SPHEREx visits taken about six months apart. A crosshair shows where the star should be, based on its known motion, and a second marker shows where we actually measured it. The Difference view subtracts visits so that only what changed remains. Users can switch between SPHEREx’s six detector arrays (0.75–5 µm), click any pixel to see its spectrum, view light curves for the variable stars, and compare the field with 2MASS, AllWISE and Gaia DR3 in a sky-context panel. Every view has its own shareable link and can be exported as a GIF. Waveshift targets movers that shift between visits months apart, such as nearby stars and brown dwarfs; asteroids and comets move within a single visit, and supporting that faster time scale is our next step.

How it works
A Python package queries SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 images from IRSA. It reprojects them onto a common 6.15″/pixel grid, masks bad pixels using the mission’s own flag planes, and stacks each visit. Curated targets are precomputed into static files, so they load instantly and keep working without a server. Custom positions go to a FastAPI service that reads only the bytes it needs from each IRSA image file. It fetches the longest wavelengths first, so cold brown dwarfs appear early, and the browser keeps refining the image in short steps. Every blank pixel is labelled with its cause: saturated, detector defect, cosmic ray, or not observed.

What’s new
Existing blink tools show motion in one or two broad bands. Waveshift combines motion with SPHEREx’s spectrum, so a mover can be checked by its colour as well as its position. Instead of a precomputed survey, it reads only the bytes it needs straight from NASA’s files, so any patch of sky works. It fetches the longest wavelengths first, so the coldest objects appear first.

Validation
Measured motion matches prediction: Barnard’s Star moved 1.68 pixels against 1.67 predicted, and Epsilon Indi B 0.98 against 1.04. WISE 0855 measures 1.65 against 1.31. That’s within the ~0.3-pixel noise at its faint signal, and by the third visit it blends with a nearby star. Static reference stars show only 0.02–0.05 pixels of false motion. Our direct file reads match IRSA’s own cutout service to about 1e-13. 103 automated tests check the pipeline.

Impact
SPHEREx photographs the whole sky every six months, but its archive is built for professional astronomers. Blink tools have already shown what the public can do with survey data: WiseView, built for the Backyard Worlds citizen-science project, has enabled hundreds of brown dwarf candidate discoveries. Waveshift brings that approach to SPHEREx, for any position on the sky rather than only our five examples, with nothing to install, no account and no astronomy software. Teachers can share a link or a GIF of a star visibly moving. Students can check the measured motion against the prediction themselves. Anyone who spots something can share the exact view with one link.

How we showed it
The 28-second video has two parts. The ~20-second opening was made and edited by hand. For the website walkthrough, we first planned to screen-record the site by hand. Instead, we wrote a script that drives the real site in Chromium with Playwright and films it one frame at a time while controlling the page’s clock. The camera moves, the cursor and the clicks in that walkthrough are all scripted, so every take is identical, renders in 4K at 60 fps, and can be re-shot in minutes after any change to the site. The live archive search plays as a time-lapse, labelled as one on screen, so the wait is shown honestly instead of cut. It cost us valuable hours in a two-day hackathon, but we think it was worth it: every bug we fixed after filming only took a re-run.

Who it’s for
We wanted the app to be usable not only by astronomers for research, but also to non-astronomers who were interested or students in the field. An early test with a non-astronomer showed us that people skim text and miss the point. So we replaced the explanation cards with a five-step guided tour pointing at the real controls, put one plain sentence above the viewer, and moved the technical controls under “More controls”.

Lasting until judging
Curated targets are precomputed into static files, so they work even if our live service goes down. The app falls back gracefully when the live service is unavailable.

Built with
Python (Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, NumPy, FastAPI, uv), TypeScript (React, Vite, Tailwind, shadcn/ui) and Aladin Lite, hosted on Vercel.
